Issued at 403 AM CDT Sat Aug 8 2026

...Mesoscale/Short Term (Today and Tonight)... 

Early morning surface mesoanalysis depicts a sagging cold front
slowly oozing southward into central Illinois. Much cooler and 
more stable air is settling in behind this boundary across 
central Iowa, where surface dewpoints have comfortably mixed 
into the mid-50s. Recent HREF guidance is in good agreement that
this front will gradually lose its identity and wash out in the
vicinity of the I-72 corridor by late afternoon.

South of this boundary, the warm sector will become moderately 
buoyant. Upper 80s surface temperatures juxtaposed with low-to-
mid 70s dewpoints and seasonably steep mid-level lapse rates 
(6-7 C/km) will yield SBCAPE values between 2000-3000 J/kg. 
Despite an uncapped warm sector environment, confidence in 
afternoon convective initiation remains remarkably low. Hi-res 
CAMs maintain a largely dry frontal passage, driven by intense 
mid-level dry air entrainment, weakening low-level convergence 
as the front washes out, and deeply nebulous upper-level 
support. Should a rogue updraft manage to overcome these 
negative factors, anomalous thermodynamics could support an 
isolated severe threat (primarily water-loaded downbursts and 
localized torrential rainfall), despite anemic deep-layer shear 
(<20 kts).


...Heat & Nocturnal Severe Threats (Sunday through Monday
Night)...

By Sunday afternoon, aggressive low-level warm air advection 
bleeding eastward from the Central Plains will force the 
remnants of today's boundary to rapidly retreat northward as a 
warm front. Central Illinois will become firmly entrenched in a 
broadening warm sector. Highs will surge into the upper 80s to 
near 90 areawide, which, when combined with mid-70s dewpoints, 
will drive heat index values to near 100F.

The convective forecast for Sunday into Sunday night remains
notoriously murky-- a classic northwest flow summertime 
dilemma. Global deterministics resolve a pronounced shortwave 
rippling along the WI/IL border Sunday morning. With the warm 
front lifting well north of the I-74 corridor, daytime 
convection should safely bypass our CWA to the north. However, 
the mesoscale evolution becomes heavily dependent on outflow 
boundaries from the morning activity. Should a composite 
outflow boundary settle south of I-80 by late Sunday afternoon, 
it would serve as a focal point for evening development. Global 
guidance advertises a secondary shortwave pushing into the 
region Sunday evening, atop a strengthening and veering low- 
level jet (LLJ). This conceptual model heavily favors a maturing
convective cold pool (MCS) organizing across northern Illinois 
and diving southward into the reservoir of greater nocturnal 
instability over our area. Understandably, CAMs are struggling 
with the spatiotemporal details of upstream initiation, keeping 
predictability quite low. However, the parameter space is 
undeniably volatile. Given the conditional risk, the SPC 
Marginal Risk for Sunday is well-placed for a late-night 
damaging wind threat.

Monday is not unlike Sunday, but with the volume turned up on 
the thermodynamics. Deep synoptic subsidence and a stout EML 
(Elevated Mixed Layer) will effectively cap the boundary layer 
through the afternoon, allowing for mostly sunny skies and 
intense diurnal heating. Afternoon highs in the low 90s and 
mid-70s dewpoints will yield extreme boundary layer buoyancy, 
with SBCAPE pushing 4500+ J/kg. The primary hazard Monday 
afternoon will be the heat, with heat index values pushing 105F 
areawide, placing us squarely in the conversation for a Heat 
Advisory. Monday night will once again feature a highly 
conditional severe threat as we watch for upstream MCS 
development tracking along the periphery of the upper ridge and 
diving south into our instability sink.


...Mid-to-Late Week (Active Flow & Pattern Shift
Uncertainty)...

The ceiling for organized severe weather appears to maximize 
Tuesday into Wednesday. A deeper, more progressive upper-level 
trough will begin digging into the Great Lakes region, buckling 
the upper-level flow and forcing a stronger belt of westerlies 
over the Midwest. This mid-level jet streak will boost 0-6 km 
bulk shear profiles into the 30-40+ kt range. When overlaid 
upon our lingering, deeply rich boundary layer moisture and 
extreme instability, the kinematic boost will strongly support 
organized convective clusters and potential bowing segments. 
Damaging winds and large hail will be the primary hazards, 
though exact mesoscale timing will depend on the evolution of 
preceding cold pools from Monday night.

anticipated, though its execution remains heavily debated among 
ensemble guidance. As the Great Lakes upper trough continues to
